newsitem.title: USA: Yamaichi revamps, rebuilds US bond business.
newsitem.headline: Yamaichi revamps, rebuilds US bond business.

text.p: Just a few months ago, layoffs and defections nearly forced Yamaichi International (America) Inc out of the U.S. government bond business.
But days before the new Japanese fiscal year begins on April 1, Yamaichi's U.S. fixed income department is close to becoming fully staffed again.

"By the end of April, we'll be able to compete for retail business," said Frank Boulton, senior executive vice president and head of fixed income at the New York-based unit of Japan's Yamaichi Securities Co.
Boulton joined Yamaichi International (America) Inc in early January, after layoffs and voluntary departures left the government bond trading staff small enough to count on one hand.

After layoffs in the fall, a mass of people quit, including such senior staff members as Patrick Lynch, head of fixed income; Nelson Thomson, head government bond trader; and executive vice president and chief economist Michael Strauss.
The departures were followed by rumors that Yamaichi was considering leaving the primary dealership business, although the firm's senior managers said they never intended to do so.

Ultimately, "they came to the conclusion that they wanted to stay as a primary dealership," Boulton told Reuters in an interview. "And I have been given a mandate to return the firm to respectibility and profitablity."

"It was never our intention to go out of (the bond) business, but I realized we had to make changes," said David Sexton, the U.S. unit's vice chairman. "But people were skeptical when I said we weren't going out of business."
Sexton said there was a "general housecleaning," as "the fixed income area needed some real hands-on attention." He hired Boulton, a former senior managing director at Smith Barney.

Boulton's first priority was to hire a staff of government bond salesmen and traders. With four to six people due to start on April 1, nearly 10 of the 14 trading positions will be filled. Meanwhile, eight of 10 salesmen have been hired.

Among recent hires on the government bond desk is new head trader Paul Devlin, who was a head trader at Smith Barney, UBS Securities and Lehman Brothers. Also hired as trades were Jim Stewart, who spent 20 years at NatWest, and Bill Shea, most recently at Nikko Securities.

Yamaichi's transformation comes at a time of fierce competition and industry consolidation. Recent years have seen a flurry of mergers, including deals between Manufacturers Hanover Bank and Chemical Bank, then Chemical and Chase Manhattan Bank; Kidder Peabody and PaineWebber; S.G. Warburg and Swiss Bank Corp; and Morgan Stanley and Dean Witter.

"I wouldn't be surprised if the industry contracted more," Boulton said. But he said Yamaichi is positioned to weather further industry turbulence, given that "we are already globalized ... If we can exercise the firm globally, we have a bright future."

He noted that Yamaichi already has established repo, collateral and emerging market trading desks. Along with revamping the government bond desk, Boulton said he also would take an "unconventional approach" to boost the mortgage-backed securities business.

Sexton said the firm looks to "beef up" its agency business and its fixed income securitization, initially in mortgages. Plus, he said he wants to increase coordination among the main Tokyo office, New York, London and Hong Kong.
"It was rocky in November," Sexton said. "But I am very pleased where where we have gotten to."
